episode_title: Season 2 – Episode 13 – Mike Lynch, Director of Sales, Stryker, talks about selling in the same territory for multiple decades

real_qa.q: How did Mike Lynch grow the Cleveland Clinic territory at Howmedica from startup to $7 million in revenue?
real_qa.r: Mike Lynch grew the Cleveland Clinic territory from $600,000 when he arrived to nearly $7 million when he left. He achieved this through value differentiation, understanding customer needs by spending the first year getting to know everyone in the organization, building relationships and trust with key decision-makers, and later adapting to the emerging RFP process. A consultant named Lester Borden helped initially, and Lynch focused on building integrity, technical expertise, and delivering results rather than just relying on personal relationships.
real_qa.requete: Mike Lynch Cleveland Clinic $7 million territory Howmedica

real_qa.q: When did Stryker start seeing RFP-driven purchasing decisions emerge at major hospital systems like Cleveland Clinic?
real_qa.r: According to Mike Lynch, RFPs started appearing around 1994-1995 at Cleveland Clinic, initially only for bipolars, with two vendors awarded contracts including Stryker and Depew. However, the real acceleration of RFP adoption among larger IDNs like UPMC and Cleveland Clinic happened in the early 2000s, fundamentally changing how sales representatives had to approach these accounts.
real_qa.requete: RFP purchasing medical device sales 1994 Cleveland Clinic

real_qa.q: What percentage of orthopedic surgeons were employed by hospitals in 2002 versus today?
real_qa.r: In 2002, only 22% of surgeons were employed by hospitals, according to Mike Lynch. Today, that percentage has risen to 80%, which is now the national average. This shift represents a fundamental change in how purchasing decisions are made, as employed surgeons have less individual autonomy compared to private practitioners.

real_qa.q: What planning and execution framework does Stryker Orthopedics Director of Sales Mike Lynch implement with his teams?
real_qa.r: Mike Lynch implements a framework combining business planning, goal-setting, and weekly planners. From each year's business plan, teams define two to four core goals—not more, because too many goals lead to ineffectiveness. Weekly planners must reflect the business plan's strategy, followed by regular cadence meetings for accountability, focusing on whether reps are executing proactively or reacting to distractions. He emphasizes managing outcomes but using process management when outcomes are missed.
real_qa.requete: sales team planning process weekly cadence accountability

real_qa.q: How should medical device sales reps prepare surgeons to advocate for their products in multi-stakeholder purchasing committees?
real_qa.r: Mike Lynch emphasizes that sales reps must 'arm your doc' with talking points relevant to financial buyers and materials managers, not just technical product details. Surgeons who attend committee meetings without economic justification will look unprepared when challenged. Sales reps need to teach their surgeon champions how to articulate value beyond product features—including quality, service, and cost-effectiveness—so they can credibly defend the choice against competing vendors.
real_qa.requete: medical device sales surgeon committee economic justification

guest.bio_context: Mike Lynch started his career in finance before transitioning to pharmaceutical sales and then medical device sales. He began with Howmedica in 1991 selling cranial plating, then moved to orthopedics where he built a territory at Cleveland Clinic from $600,000 to nearly $7 million over 10 years. He progressed through roles including Northeast Ohio Area Manager for Stryker Three Rivers in 2002 and VP of Sales in 2006, and has been in medical device sales for 30 years. He is married to his wife Ann for 32 years and has two grown daughters.
